headline: New Haven Break Gives Up Jumbo Porgies While Charles Island Bar Holds Bass After Dark
subhead: Bottom fishing is peaking on the rockpiles as the tide eases toward neap — but the stripers want you out there when the sun's down.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning, outer New Haven breakwall, high skimmer rig loaded with sandworm, and a porgy comes up that makes the guy next to me put his rod down just to look at it. Better than a pound and a half, flank flashing gold in the sun, and he's grinning like he just found money in an old coat. That's the breakwall in early August for you — you never know when the next drop is going to be the fish of the trip.

This is peak season on the rockpiles right now and it's not subtle. Porgies are stacked on the New Haven Harbor breakwalls in 15 to 20 feet, thickest on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high water, when the current slacks enough that a light skimmer rig with squid strips or sandworm actually sits still on the bottom instead of getting dragged sideways. I've been running 1/2-ounce sinkers on 12-pound braid, small hooks, size 4 or 6 — bigger porgies are surprisingly leader-shy this time of year and a bulky rig gets you fewer bites. Sea bass are mixed right in with them, especially out toward the tip of the outer wall where the rock drops into deeper water. Squid and clam belly are still the ticket, and the keepers have been running 14 to 16 inches with enough shorts in the mix that you're working for your limit, not filling a bucket in twenty minutes.

Falkner Island has been the more consistent sea bass spot the last two weeks — the rockpile structure off the northeast side in 25 to 30 feet is holding fish that don't seem to care much what the tide's doing, though the bite sharpens noticeably on the last of the ebb when bait gets pulled off the structure and the bass bunch up to intercept it. Bring bucktails with a squid teaser trailer if you want to cover ground instead of just soaking bait — you'll pick off the more aggressive fish that way and save your clams for the pickier ones.

Stratford Shoal is fishing the way Stratford Shoal always fishes in high summer — good porgy and sea bass numbers on the rockier stretches, but the current there is honest and unforgiving, and this week it's actually working in our favor. We're sliding into a neap tide around August 5th and 6th, and the softer swing means less sinker weight, cleaner drifts, and a lot more precision when you're trying to hold a bait tight against a specific piece of structure instead of getting swept off it every fifteen minutes. If you've been frustrated fishing the Shoal on a big tide, this is your window — go lighter, feel the bottom better, and you'll catch more fish for the same effort.

As for tog — we're still in the summer closure, so if you're marking fish tight to the rock piles at Falkner or the Charles Island reef, admire them and move on. That fishery comes back in a few weeks and it'll be worth the wait.

Now the striper story is a different animal entirely, and it's exactly the story we flagged last week — that as the tides soften into the neap, bass would stop roaming and compress onto the deepest, coolest structure, feeding hardest in the tightest current windows. That's precisely what's setting up on the sandbar off Charles Island right now. Water's sitting in the mid-to-upper 70s on the surface, which means daytime bass are holding deep, tucked against the drop-off on the north side of the bar, mostly uninterested in anything you throw at them until the sun starts to go down. But from last light through the first couple hours of dark, on the last of the outgoing when bait gets pulled off the flat and funnels along that sandbar edge, the bass come up and they come up hungry. Live eels have been the most consistent producer — slow-troll them along the drop or drift them back on a fish-finder rig — with bucktails in white or chartreuse picking up fish on the retrieve when there's current to work with. Nothing enormous yet, mostly 26 to 32 inches, but a few overslot fish have shown in the mix for guys willing to fish the full dark hours instead of packing it in at dusk.

Bluefish remain entirely a bait story this month. Wherever bunker pods have been holding — and they've been moving around off Hammonasset and occasionally pushing up toward the Milford Gulf — the blues show up within hours and it turns into topwater chaos for as long as the bait stays put. It's not a spot you can circle on a chart and count on; it's a spot you find by watching the birds and the surface nervous water that morning. Bring wire leader and something loud — a Hopkins jig or a bunker spoon — because when they're on the bait they're not fussy.

Fluke have been the quiet steady performer over sand pockets around the Milford Gulf and off Hammonasset in 15 to 25 feet, working the moving water with 4-inch white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails dragged slow along bottom. Nothing gigantic, but a legal fish or two most drifts if you're patient about covering ground.

Looking ahead: with the neap easing current everywhere, I'd spend the next several days on the rockpiles — porgies and sea bass should stay strong and the lighter tide makes for more comfortable, more precise fishing. For stripers, plan around the last two hours of light and the first couple hours of dark at Charles Island; that's where the fish are concentrating and where the effort actually pays off right now.
